title: Gandhari
hook: a folded cloth, tied once over a young bride's eyes, and the many ways people have read it since

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari's answer to her son before battle: where dharma is, there is victory.

Paintings show it. So do films and television. A strip of cloth, tied over Gandhari's eyes. Last year on this path, the story of how it got there was told in passing: a princess of Gandhara learns that the prince she will marry, Dhritarashtra, is blind, and she binds her own eyes. The Mahabharata tells it in a few lines and moves on. Readers have kept coming back to it. Today: Gandhari's blindfold, and the different things people see in it.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `A FEW LINES IN THE EPIC.` → `WHAT PEOPLE SEE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what the first book of the Mahabharata gives, in paraphrase. Gandhari hears that her husband-to-be is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it over, and binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband. That's it. No speech. No explanation beyond that one resolve. Readers have filled the silence in different ways. Devotional retellings hear devotion: a wife who would not see what her husband could not, and the strength the stories give her for it. Others hear solidarity, sharing his darkness rather than looking down on it. And some modern readers hear something more troubled: a woman of clear sight who chose not to look, at a court that badly needed someone to look. Those readings sit side by side; the epic doesn't settle them. There's also a story from later retellings. Before his last fight, Gandhari asks Duryodhana to come to her unclothed, so that one look from her long-covered eyes can make his body hard as diamond. He comes, but out of shame covers his waist, and that is where he is struck. It's a story about the power people sensed behind the cloth. A choice made once can shape a whole life. A sacrifice can be read many ways at once, and the person making it doesn't control the reading. And the cloth isn't the end of Gandhari's sight. In the war's aftermath she will see in other ways, and that is tomorrow's story.
screen: `SHE FOLDS A CLOTH OVER HER EYES` · `DEVOTION, SOLIDARITY, OR NOT LOOKING` · `A STORY OF A DIAMOND BODY` · `ONE CHOICE, MANY READINGS`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere safe, close your eyes or rest a hand gently over them, and notice how the room changes: the sounds come closer, the body gets louder. After a few breaths, ask one quiet question, whether there's something in your life you've chosen not to look at, and without opening it now, just notice whether something answers before you let your eyes open slowly. If you pray, you can ask to see clearly.
Gandhari. Hearing her husband was blind, she bound her own eyes, and readers since have seen devotion, solidarity and refusal in that one cloth. Today's word.
Your line: Gandhari. One folded cloth, and so many ways of reading it. Until tomorrow.

notes: Confirm the Adi Parva lines: Gandhari folds a cloth many times and binds her eyes, resolving not to exceed (atyasuya) her husband. Section numbers differ between editions.
